summary: Image classification predicts one or more class labels for an entire image.
detail: For a photo of fruit, a classifier might decide whether it shows an apple or a banana. Outputs are usually scores or probabilities for each class, describing what the image depicts overall.

summary: Object detection identifies both the locations and the classes of objects in an image.
detail: In a street photo, a detector might draw separate boxes around three cars and two pedestrians. Each result usually includes a bounding box, class, and confidence score for counting or subsequent tracking.

summary: Semantic segmentation assigns a semantic class to every pixel in an image.
detail: In a road scene, pixels might be labeled as road, vehicle, or sky. Two adjacent cars can share the same class label: the output describes which class each region belongs to.

summary: Instance segmentation identifies individual objects and the pixels occupied by each one.
detail: For three cups on a table, the model produces a separate mask for each cup. This captures their outlines and distinguishes which pixels belong to which cup.

summary: Panoptic segmentation assigns a class to every pixel and instance identities to objects that need to be distinguished individually.
detail: A street scene needs complete labels for road and sky as well as separate identities for each pedestrian and car. Panoptic segmentation combines these outputs into a single pixel-level annotation.

summary: Object tracking locates objects across successive video frames while maintaining their identities.
detail: Single-object tracking follows a specified target; multi-object tracking (MOT) must also distinguish targets and maintain their identities. Frame-by-frame detection, motion prediction, and appearance matching are common components. Occlusion and reappearance make identity association harder.

summary: Depth estimation predicts distances within a scene or relative depth at locations in an image.
detail: A depth map is a representation of the estimate, rather than the estimation method. Monocular models may predict relative depth or metric depth under particular training and calibration conditions; stereo cameras and depth sensors provide extra geometric information. Compare results using explicit units, scales, and coordinate conventions.

summary: Pose estimation infers the position, orientation, or structural keypoints of a person, object, or camera.
detail: Human pose can be represented by a skeleton connecting shoulders, elbows, wrists, and other keypoints. A robot grasping a cup may instead need its three-dimensional position and orientation. Different tasks use different pose representations.

summary: Optical flow describes the direction and distance of apparent movement of pixels or image features between consecutive images.
detail: When a ball moves to the right, flow vectors near it point rightward. Camera movement also produces optical flow, so the flow reflects both scene motion and changes in viewpoint.

summary: An image patch is a small local region cut from an image, often used as a basic input unit in vision models.
detail: An image can be divided into a fixed-size grid, with each patch converted to a visual token. Smaller patches generally preserve more positional detail but produce longer sequences.

summary: A feature map arranges feature responses over spatial positions, often across multiple channels.
detail: A convolutional output commonly has channel, height, and width dimensions. Channels contain different learned features; they are not necessarily recognizable edges or object classes, and the feature map is not the input image.

summary: A bounding box represents an object's location and extent using a rectangle or another specified box format.
detail: Two-dimensional detection often uses top-left and bottom-right coordinates, or a center point with width and height. Boxes support localization and counting; following an irregular contour such as a cup handle precisely requires a pixel-level mask.

summary: A segmentation mask marks the pixels covered by an object or region.
detail: Marking person pixels as 1 and background pixels as 0 produces a binary person mask. Masks can support background removal or indicate which areas an image editing model should modify.

summary: A keypoint is one of a small set of representative locations used to describe object structure or match images.
detail: Wrists and knees on a body, or eye corners and the nose tip on a face, can serve as semantic keypoints. Their locations support motion estimation, face alignment, or tracking of local movement.

summary: A convolutional neural network learns representations using shared local convolutions and can process images, audio, and other locally structured data.
detail: Early layers can respond to edges and simple textures, while later layers combine local information into more complex structures. Reusing a convolutional kernel's parameters across locations lets the network look for similar patterns throughout an image.

summary: ViT splits an image into patches, turns them into a sequence, and uses a Transformer to learn relationships between patches.
detail: Each patch is mapped to a vector and supplied with positional information. Attention lets distant patches exchange information, for example connecting wheels, windows, and a car body into a whole vehicle.

summary: A vision backbone converts raw images into feature representations for downstream tasks.
detail: A detector can use ResNet or ViT to extract information about edges, textures, and object structure before task-specific modules predict boxes and classes. The backbone extracts visual features that task-specific modules can share.
sourceTitles: Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection

summary: A vision neck connects a backbone to task heads by organizing or fusing visual features at different scales.
detail: Small objects require precise location information, while large objects require semantic information spanning a larger area. Structures such as FPN combine features from different layers so a detection head can use multiple scales.
sourceTitles: Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection

summary: A vision head converts feature representations into predictions for a particular task.
detail: The same backbone can feed a classification head, bounding box regression head, or mask head. The task determines the output format and training target, such as class scores or a foreground probability for every pixel.

summary: A receptive field is the region of an input image that can influence a particular feature location.
detail: Recognizing a thin line may require only a small window, while recognizing a whole car requires a larger region. The number of convolutional layers, kernel sizes, and downsampling choices affect the receptive field.

summary: Convolution scans local regions with shared weights to produce features that respond to particular local patterns.
detail: A convolutional kernel is a set of weights; convolution is the operation that applies them. Visual networks reuse the weights across locations to produce feature maps. Deep learning libraries commonly use cross-correlation without flipping the kernel while still calling the layer a convolution.

summary: Pooling summarizes local features into fewer values, often to reduce the spatial size of a feature map.
detail: Max pooling keeps the largest response in a small region; average pooling takes the mean. Smaller spatial dimensions reduce subsequent computation while also compressing some positional detail.

summary: Non-maximum suppression reduces duplicate detection boxes by retaining high-scoring candidates and removing excessively overlapping ones.
detail: A detector might draw five similar boxes around one cup. NMS usually keeps the highest-scoring box first, removes duplicates using an overlap threshold, and repeats the process on the remaining boxes.
